transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

As soon as I know I have to go up high on a building, I get an overwhelming rush of fear the moment I even approach the scaffolding. It's been happening at my construction job, and I really need some help with it.
Can you tell me if this fear of heights is interfering with your daily life or is it primarily a problem when you're at work on the construction site?

It's primarily at work, but it's having a huge impact on my life because it's ruining my career and my finances. I've had to turn down overtime, I skipped a major training tower test, and now I'm getting passed over for the promotions and supervisory roles I've worked so hard for. It's just incredibly frustrating because it's holding me back from making a decent living.

Can you describe how you feel when you're in a situation where you're not in a high place, but you know you'll have to go to a high place later, such as when you're getting ready for work or traveling to a construction site?

Just knowing I have to go up high gets my body freaking out before I even touch a ladder. My chest tightens, my heart starts racing, and my legs feel completely wobbly just seeing the scaffolding or hearing we're going to be on a high floor. Sometimes that dread is so bad that it keeps me from showing up to work at all.

Have you found yourself avoiding not just the heights at work, but also other situations or activities in your personal life that involve heights, such as hiking or being in a high-rise building for leisure?

I haven't really thought about it or run into those situations in my free time, to be honest. My mind has been completely focused on just trying to get through my shifts at work, so the scaffolding on the construction sites is really the only place I've had to deal with this.

Can you tell me if you've experienced any significant anxiety or fear in social situations, such as meeting new people, being in crowds, or feeling judged by others, outside of your work-related height anxieties?
No, I don't experience any anxiety or fear in social situations, meeting new people, or being in crowds. My anxiety is strictly related to heights and having to go up on that scaffolding at work.
Can you tell me if your fear of heights is specifically triggered by the fear of falling, or is it more about the feeling of being in a high place itself, regardless of any safety measures in place?

It’s a mix of both, but even with all the safety gear on, standing on those open metal planks with nothing solid around me is terrifying. I get this awful feeling like I’m about to slide right off the edge. It’s crazy because everyone else is walking around up there like it’s no big deal, but it just completely panics me.

Is your fear of heights only triggered by the actual presence of heights, or does even thinking about or imagining yourself in a high place, without any immediate danger of falling, provoke a significant anxiety response?

Yes, absolutely. Just the idea of standing on those open metal planks or hearing that we have to work on a high floor is enough to trigger it. My chest tightens, my heart starts racing, and my legs feel wobbly before I even set foot on a ladder.

Have you ever experienced a full-blown panic attack, where you felt like you were going to pass out, have a heart attack, or completely lose control, when confronted with a high place or even just thinking about it?

Yes, it definitely feels like my body is completely freaking out. My chest tightens, my heart starts racing, and my legs shake so badly that I end up freezing halfway up the ladder, just clinging to the rails. It's an overwhelming rush of physical panic every single time.

Can you describe the duration of these panic episodes when you're confronted with heights or even just thinking about them, and do they resolve once you're away from the high place or the thought of it?

I'm not sure of the exact number of minutes, but those intense feelings like my racing heart and shaking generally last as long as I'm near the edge or facing the height. They do start to calm down and go away once I'm safely back on the ground.
